column3: It directly repeats appointed leaders who guide by the divine command, adding patience and certainty as their formation.
The request for sound judgment and righteous company only distantly frames the qualities associated with guidance.
It shows a community guiding and judging by truth, extending the focus from appointed leaders to a just guided collectivity.
It presents the same prophetic household as hurrying to good works, calling in hope and fear, and being humble.
The gift of criterion and remembrance supplies a limited revelation backdrop for the command guiding the leaders.
It supplies the inverse boundary: clear signs can be knowingly rejected, after which guidance is not granted.
It closely matches the focus's established prayer and almsgiving while showing their resilience amid commerce and judgment-consciousness.
As immediate context, it identifies Abraham and Lot's rescue to blessed land before the later appointment of the household.
It retains prayer, almsgiving, and obedience as a durable communal practice after an earlier specific demand is lifted.
It reiterates guidance and justice as a collective pattern, though it adds little beyond the earlier parallel.
As immediate context, it identifies Isaac and Jacob as righteous, clarifying those included in the focus's plural appointment.
It repeats the prayer-and-almsgiving practice and adds obedience to the messenger as its merciful orientation.
It shows revealed instruction organizing a vulnerable community's homes around prayer.
A believer's call to follow him toward right conduct gives a concrete human form to guiding others.
It preserves the paired establishment of prayer and giving of alms, grounding them in certainty about the final return.
It supplies the direct inverse of the focus: leaders can call toward the Fire rather than guide by divine command.

It distinguishes the divine command's source from its delivery through chosen servants.
It connects faith, prayer, almsgiving, and fear of God with sustaining a shared worship space.

It joins established prayer with open and hidden spending before the irreversible day.
It explicitly joins the lifting of the oppressed with making them leaders and heirs, a close political counterpart to the focus.
It makes prayer, almsgiving, command of good, and restraint of wrong the test of authority in the land.
It provides a concise early pairing of prayer, almsgiving, and collective bowing, now largely redundant.
It places prayer and almsgiving within a fuller account of faithful, costly, and steadfast good action.
In the immediate sequence, the blessed reminder supplies the revealed basis from which Abraham's guidance proceeds.
Its general designation of revelation as guidance and good news adds little detail to the focus.
It concentrates sincere worship, prayer, and almsgiving into an explicitly commanded religious practice.
The scene of enduring desired reward does not clarify leadership, commanded good works, or communal worship.
The warning to an unalerted people provides only a distant precondition for guidance.
It portrays rescued believers being made successors after rejection, offering a parallel of succession following deliverance.

The settling of every matter has only a formal connection to acting by divine command.
The revelation to Joseph amid danger offers only a remote instance of divine instruction.
The immediate denial that creation is play gives a broad purposive backdrop but no specific account of the focus's practices.
It distinguishes conveying a reminder from forcing purification, a limited boundary on guided action.
The succession of rejected messengers gives only a general historical backdrop for guided communities.
It presents every creature as knowing and performing its own prayer and glorification, broadening worship as enacted knowledge.
It contrasts claimed self-purification with purification that belongs to God.
It joins belief, public moral direction, and haste in good works within a righteous community.
The immediate account of inherited idol worship marks the false devotional allegiance opposed by Abraham's guided household.
Maintaining what God commands to be joined gives a limited example of carrying divine order into social relations.
It reinforces active haste in good works, though that contribution is already supplied by the closer household parallel.
This later episode of repentance and invocation has only a secondary relation to worshipful prophetic action.
It repeats prayer, almsgiving, and certainty but is redundant after several fuller formulations.
It links almsgiving, reverent restraint, and faith in signs to a specifically received mercy.
The conclusion that such people are upon guidance adds little beyond the preceding practice description.
Warning as a means by which a people may be guided is only a general antecedent to the focus.
It gives a revealed command that directs Moses toward protective communal action.
The immediate naming of manifest error sharpens the contrast between Abraham's truth-guided stance and inherited devotion.
It gives the negative limit that persistent corruption is not repaired by a guide's intercession.
The divine bestowal of apparent goods is not the focus's human performance of good works.
It shows obedient servants who do not precede God in speech and act by His command, a close model of authorized action.
Standing firmly for justice is a useful ethical echo but does not directly develop the focus's leadership or worship pattern.
The destruction of Noah's people offers a remote warning context rather than a positive account of guided leadership.
Prepared paths in the earth provide only a figurative and general account of finding guidance.
It clarifies giving wealth as an act of purification, contributing a specific dimension of the focus's almsgiving.
The command to Moses to act against deception is a distant instance of revelation becoming action.
The immediate question about truth versus play advances the idol episode but adds little to the focus's practices.
It gives an inverse leadership outcome: a people can be brought into ruin through the misuse of divine favor.
The immediate designation of the message as communication for worshippers directly echoes the focus's concluding worship.
The defeat of Abraham's plotters is nearby narrative context but does not explain the later appointment.
Prophethood and scripture in Abraham's and Noah's descendants form a broad lineage backdrop without the focus's practice pattern.
Representative selection and testing show that communal guidance is not mechanically transferred through chosen members.
It combines established prayer with public moral instruction and patience, giving a durable personal form of guided action.
Moses' invitation to Pharaoh's purification preserves voluntary response but is distant from the focus's communal order.
It places revealed judgment, distinct communal paths, and striving in good works within one accountable religious order.
The immediate confession of the Creator and witness establishes Abraham's truth claim but not the focus's institutional practices.
It repeats prayer and almsgiving with a future return of good, but adds little after earlier parallels.
The instruction to Moses' mother offers a remote example of revelation prompting protective action.
The later fragmentation of religious affairs supplies a contrast to leaders maintaining a coherent guided order.
It links uncorrupted faith with security and guidance, but only at a general level.
Prayer-centered settlement and provision offer a secondary communal setting, now redundant for the focus.
Human dependence on God does not materially clarify the focus's appointed guidance or named practices.
Steadfast testimony is a limited public analogue to reliably maintaining a commanded order.
The food request and its aftermath do not materially develop the focus's leadership, worship, or good works.
The immediate resolve to confront idols is narrative context but does not add to the focus's positive account of leadership.
The statement that God guides whom He wills remains too general to illuminate the specific guided practices.
The terse description of faith and reverent restraint adds no distinct detail beyond earlier cards.
Truth's defeat of falsehood is a nearby thematic backdrop, not an explanation of the appointed leaders' work.
It makes almsgiving an active doing, giving concise support to the focus's pairing of revelation and good works.
The disavowal of false patrons and forgotten remembrance gives only a contrast to proper worship.
It presents an individual believer defending truth amid Pharaoh's court, but offers little about the focus's institutions.
Human failure to fulfill the command is a general negative counterpart to the focus's enacted obedience.
It limits any inference that closeness to righteous servants guarantees a person's own right standing.
The immediate breaking of idols aims at return and correction, but adds little to the later leadership formula.
It explicitly joins Quranic guidance to righteous deeds, giving a text-centered source for the focus's guided action.
The designation of leaders of disbelief supplies another direct inverse to the focus's righteous leaders.
Life from water offers a broad creation backdrop with no close contribution to guided leadership or worship.
It warns against carrying scripture without enacting it, a limited negative contrast to revealed good works.
It depicts a people divided into communities with known provision under Mosaic revelation, a secondary model of organized communal care.
The same sign guiding some and exposing others gives a general response-dependent boundary for guidance.
Moses and Aaron's mission to Pharaoh provides only a broad prophetic precedent.
It calls the earlier scripture an imam and mercy, adding the textual sense of a guiding reference point.
The appeal to divine will and inherited practice contrasts with accountable response, but only distantly.
It repeats prayer, almsgiving, obedience, and purification in a domestic setting, now substantially redundant.
Prayer joined with patience supplies a limited personal resource for sustaining obedience.
It marks responsive belief as a condition for hearing to become guidance, a general boundary rather than a close parallel.
Secure carved dwellings do not clarify the focus's leaders, guidance, or worship practices.
It gives leadership an eschatological public dimension while preserving each person's individual accountability.
It is the clearest omitted appointment of Abraham as an imam, while limiting that covenant to descendants who do not commit wrong.
Abraham's prayer for a messenger who recites, teaches, and purifies gives an Abrahamic program for forming a guided community.
It joins the messenger's recitation and teaching with purification, supplying a formative route toward the focus's enacted good.
It requires a community that calls to good, commands what is recognized, and restrains what is wrong.
The sending of a messenger who recites, purifies, and teaches shows guidance as communal formation rather than mere information.
The gift of scripture, wisdom, and great authority to Abraham's family supplies a close lineage backdrop for their appointment.
It orders obedience to God, the messenger, and those entrusted with authority, framing leadership within accountable return to revelation.
It portrays revealed scripture as guidance and light, with prophets and learned custodians judging by what God revealed.
It combines allegiance, prayer, almsgiving, and bowing in a compact account of a faithful communal order.
The gift of scripture, judgment, and prophethood to a prophetic company supplies a close resource base for divinely guided leadership.
It directs following the guidance of the preceding prophets, making their guidance a transmissible pattern.
Moses charges Aaron to succeed among the people, act rightly, and avoid the corrupters, directly joining succession with moral stewardship.
It makes allied believing men and women sustain prayer, almsgiving, obedience, and public moral direction together.
It assigns part of the community to gain understanding and warn their people, adding an organized teaching role to guidance.
The universal messenger charge to worship God and avoid false objects of devotion provides the basic direction leaders must transmit.
Its command of justice, good, and giving to kin gives a concise ethical content for the focus's revealed good works.
It joins blessing with the continuing obligation of prayer and almsgiving in a prophetic life.
It explicitly depicts Ishmael commanding his people to prayer and almsgiving while being pleasing to his Lord.
The command to establish prayer for remembrance gives a foundational purpose for the practice named in the focus.
It commands sustained prayer within the household and patience in maintaining it, closely paralleling the focus's institutional worship.
As the immediate continuation of the Abraham cycle, it gives Lot judgment and knowledge and rescues him from corrupt communal practice.
It completes the nearby prophetic pattern by placing Noah among the righteous admitted to mercy.
It states that the earth is inherited by God's righteous servants, a direct horizon for righteous communal leadership.
It calls the chosen community to prayer, almsgiving, and holding fast to God, extending the focus's practices to collective vocation.
It promises succession, establishment, and secure worship to those who believe and do good works, closely integrating the focus's themes.
The prayer to be made an imam for the reverent adds a requested, exemplary form of leadership.
It places prophethood and scripture in Abraham's descendants, supplying a lineage context for the focus's Abrahamic household.
David's appointment as a successor with the charge to judge by truth gives a governance-specific counterpart to divinely directed leadership.
It presents the establishment of religion as the shared charge of the major prophetic line, placing the focus in a continuous commission.
It describes revelation as a spirit by which the messenger guides to a straight path, directly linking revelation and guidance.
Jesus brings wisdom and calls people to worship God, pairing clarified judgment with shared devotional direction.
It joins messengers, scripture, balance, and people's standing for justice, giving the public-justice dimension of guided leadership.
It describes the messenger reciting signs, purifying, and teaching scripture and wisdom to form a people from prior error.
It again joins established prayer, almsgiving, and voluntary good, emphasizing their sustained practice under changing circumstances.
It links purification, remembrance of the Lord, and prayer in a concise devotional sequence.
